🌟The Heart of Washington Hills: A Leader Who Leads by Serving! At Washington Hills Community Center, leadership means more than managing a facility. For Center Manager Shay Smith, it means building relationships, showing up for residents, and being willing to step into whatever role is needed. Whether she's on the basketball court, participating in a line dancing class, or simply checking in with someone who walks through the doors, Smith believes community building starts with genuine connections. Smith began her career with the City in 1998 as a part-time summer employee. Over 25 years, she served at several community centers, including Carver, Chris L. Ramsey Sr., East Lake, South Chattanooga, Tyner, and East Chattanooga, before becoming the manager at Washington Hills. Inspired by mentors like her "second mother," Mama Lexine, Smith saw firsthand how investing in young people could positively influence an entire neighborhood. Those experiences helped shape her commitment to public service and continue to guide her work today. "This job is something you have to want to do," Smith shares. "A degree doesn't make you want to do this. I had opportunities to take jobs that made more money, but I chose this work because I like seeing people grow and helping people." For Smith, serving residents often means going beyond her everyday responsibilities. Throughout her career, she has helped neighborhood youth get to job interviews, connected residents with assistance, and created opportunities for children to experience life beyond their immediate surroundings. From organizing trips to Atlanta to taking young people to local sporting events, she believes exposing children to new experiences can open their eyes to possibilities they may not have considered. Smith's leadership philosophy is built on leading by example. She believes no task is beneath a leader and makes it a priority to work alongside her staff. "When I get out of my car, I'm the custodian, I'm the rec spec, I'm the facility manager," says Smith. "If you're on my team, I'm never going to ask you to do something you haven't seen me do." After more than two decades of service, Smith's passion remains rooted in the people she serves. Whether supporting senior programs, providing recreational opportunities for youth, or simply lending a helping hand, she measures success by the relationships she builds and the lives she touches. "To help meet the needs of whoever comes through that door—that's where my joy and my peace come from," Smith reflects. "When people come back years later to say thank you, that's what does it for me." For Smith, that's what community development is all about: showing up, investing in people, and making a difference one relationship at a time.

Thanksgiving Rescue: On 11/26/26 at 1:16 AM, Engine 9 Blue Shift was dispatched to the 2500 block of Westside Drive on a motor vehicle crash with the car possibly being down an embankment. With this information, Engine 9 started two squad companies for possible extrication. E9 arrived on scene with multiple CPD units and EMS. Firefighters found the car approximately 50 feet down the embankment. E9 advised Squad 1 and Squad 13 that a Stokes basket and a rope system would be needed to extricate the patient. S1 and S13 arrived on scene and started to build the haul system and the Stokes basket to lower down to first responders with the patient. The basket was lowered down and the patient was secured in the basket. The basket was hauled up and once at the top, the patient was transferred over to EMS. Strong work by everyone involved in this overnight  rescue.

Have you noticed some new visitors in some of our parks lately? This is BORDERS, a public installation by artist Steinunn Thórarinsdóttir. Twenty-two life-sized figures, half cast iron, half aluminum, stand and sit in silent conversation. Though made of contrasting materials, their androgynous forms are identical. They create invisible borders meant to be crossed, inviting strangers to step in, sit down, and connect. These figures have traveled across the country, from New York and Chicago to here in Coolidge Park and Montague Park Sculpture Fields. A quiet reminder that despite our outward differences, we share the exact same humanity. Head out to the parks, take a seat beside them, and see how you connect—don’t forget to share your photos and tag Sculpture Fields and CreativeEconCha!

⚠ November is #StrangulationAwarenessMonth  The "Choking Game," which is often framed as a harmless thrill or viral challenge, involves intentionally restricting oxygen to the brain to achieve a temporary "high." But cutting off oxygen to the brain is not a game. In just seconds, oxygen deprivation causes brain cells to die. A few minutes of giving into peer pressure or trying a online challenge can lead to permanent traumatic brain injury, memory loss, seizures, motor skill impairment, or death. Talk to the young people in your life about the real physical dangers of oxygen deprivation and the pressure to participate in dangerous trends. Brain damage is irreversible and no trend is worth a life. Learn more: https://www.allianceforhope.org/resources/the-choking-game #allianceforhopeinternational #FamilyJusticeCenter #TheLastWarningShot #StrangulationAwarenessMonth  #EndDomesticViolence #KnowTheSigns

This position will also analyze and resolve network related hardware and software problems in a timely and accurate fashion and provide training where required to support the team. SERIES LEVEL: The Network Engineer Lead is second level in a two-level network engineering series. ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS: (The following duties ARE NOT intended to serve as a comprehensive list of all duties performed by all employees in this classification, only a representative summary of the primary duties and responsibilities. Incumbent(s) may not be required to perform all duties listed and may be required to perform additional, position-specific duties.) Manage numerous concurrent tasks and assignments, with frequent interruptions. Assist and mentor team members during the duration of an assignment or project when necessary. Serve as a subject matter expert for all networking. Install software and hardware on networking equipment and microcomputers as directed. Deploy LANs, WANs, and wireless networks, including routers, switches, firewalls, and other hardware. Ensure upgrades of all network hardware and related software are performed in a timely manner. Coordinate with third-party vendors for installations. Planning of new network build-outs and refreshing of equipment and cabling. Monitor network performance and troubleshoot problem areas as needed. Maintain network performance history and provide network performance statistics and reports. Perform network asset management, including maintenance of network component inventory and related documentation and technical specifications information. Perform all job responsibilities in alignment with the industry’s best security practices and regulatory guidelines to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of protected information and other sensitive data. Assist with purchasing and acquisition of network components and services. Assist the Manager Network Operations with short-term planning and long-term planning for network operations; work with end-users to understand utilization and networking needs. Assist with the development of procedures and standards pertaining to network operations. Receive, prepare, and process a variety of reports, correspondence, inventories, and other documentation as necessary to carry out job responsibilities and comply with departmental or city procedures. Participate in/on a variety of meetings, conferences, training sessions, and/or other related groups in order to receive and convey information. Be available during the normal business hours, and may occasionally be asked to vary their schedule and/or work overtime to meet department requirements. Work will generally be performed using computer equipment in and indoor office environment. Some work will require outdoor configurations and installation. Setup or maintenance of some peripheral equipment may require work in areas such as data rooms or wiring closets with restricted room for movement. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers, and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. Performs other duties as assigned. It takes split-second coordination and immense courage to pull someone from a burning vehicle—and on the night of November 6, 2026, Squad 13 Green Shift crew delivered when it mattered most. CPD Arrests Two People In Roanoke Ave Homicide CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) has arrested two people in connection to a homicide on Roanoke Avenue. At approximately 8:30 a.m. on November 17, 2026 officers responded to reports of a deceased person in the 1800 block of Roanoke Avenue. Upon arrival, officers located a 24-year-old man with multiple gunshot wounds. He was pronounced dead at the scene. CPD's Crime Scene and Homicide Units responded to process and investigate the scene. The preliminary investigation indicates the suspect, Qence Burgess (DOB: 12/12/2002), was dropped off, waited for the victim, and shot him. During an interview, Burgess confessed to the shooting. He is charged with First Degree Murder and Tampering with Evidence. A second suspect, Jessica Williams (DOB: 2/10/1982), is charged with Facilitation of First Degree Murder. Both suspects were transported to the Hamilton County Jail.  This remains an active and ongoing investigation. This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. The Chattanooga Police Department asks anyone with information about this incident to call (423) 698-2525. The charges and allegations referenced in this release are merely accusations of criminal conduct and not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted through due process of law. #CPDnews

It was about standing with families, showing support for those impacted, reminding residents that they are not forgotten, and making it clear that gun violence will not define the future of our communities. Real change requires collective action. It requires partnership, compassion, accountability, and a community willing to stand together. We will continue to show up, speak out, build relationships, and work toward safer neighborhoods for everyone. One Community. One Voice. Paul Feaster regularly visits the Hixson Community Center to enjoy pickleball and connect with fellow residents. With more than 40 years of experience as a paramedic, Paul understands how critical it is to have the right equipment available during a medical emergency. During a competitive game of pickleball, he recognized that the center's existing first-aid resources were not sufficient to provide potentially life-saving assistance while waiting for emergency responders to arrive. Rather than simply raising a concern, Paul took action. He met with Hixson Community Center Manager Kevin McGowan and spoke with City Council members to advocate for accessible Automated External Defibrillators (AEDs) in community centers. His advocacy sparked an important conversation and became a priority for the Department of Community Development. As a result of Paul's call to action, the department made it a mission to ensure AEDs were installed and accessible in every Chattanooga community center, helping create safer spaces for the residents who visit them every day. Hear Paul's story and learn how one resident's initiative helped move the needle to make a life-saving difference across our community.

River City Company, in partnership with the Indigenous Public Art Committee and Public Art Chattanooga, is seeking Indigenous artists and artist-led teams for two permanent public art commissions as part of the Riverfront Parks NEXT project in Downtown Chattanooga. The selected artists will have the opportunity to create works at Ross's Landing, a site known to the Cherokee and Creek as Atla'nuwa or Tsatanugi. This location holds deep historical and cultural significance for more than 23 Tribal Nations and serves as a crossroads of ancestral homelands and living cultures. The hike is rated as moderate, as the ground can be uneven with rocks and has two gradual climbs and two descents totaling about 350 feet in elevation gain/loss. 📜 Thank you, Hamilton County! 💗 Hamilton County Mayor Weston Wamp has officially proclaimed November 2026 as Family Court Awareness Month for the fifth year! We are grateful to Mayor Wamp for recognizing that children’s safety must be the central consideration in our family courts, especially in cases involving abuse or violence. Why does this matter? Family courts make life-changing decisions about divorce, custody, visitation, dependency and neglect, and domestic violence. And the stakes are high: 🔹 The Leadership Council on Child Abuse and Interpersonal Violence estimates that more than 58,000 children each year are ordered into unsupervised contact with physically or sexually abusive parents after divorce. 🔹 The Center for Judicial Excellence has documented hundreds of children killed by a parent or parental figure in cases involving divorce, separation, custody, visitation, or child support. 🔹 The period after separation can bring heightened danger for domestic violence victims and their children. 💗 Wear Hot Pink on Wednesday, November 18! 💗 Hamilton County also recognizes the third Wednesday of November as Hot Pink Day. Wear pink in recognition of the children whose safety and well-being are affected by family court proceedings, and to remember those we’ve lost.  Share your photo and tag us! HAPPY BIRTHDAY, CFD: The Chattanooga Fire Department marks 155 years of continuous service today, celebrating a legacy that began in the ashes of the post-Civil War era and evolved into one of Tennessee’s premier modern emergency response organizations. Prior to 1871, fire protection in Chattanooga relied on loosely organized volunteer bucket brigades and early hand-drawn pumpers. As the city rapidly transformed into a major railroad and industrial hub following the Civil War, timber-framed buildings, crowded rail yards, and expanding manufacturing plants created fire hazards that outpaced volunteer capacity. On November 14, 1871, the Chattanooga Fire Department (CFD) was formed. City leaders formally established a paid department, commissioning Engine Company No. 1. Equipped with steam-powered fire engines pulled by teams of trained fire horses, the fledgling department laid the foundation for organized, full-time municipal fire protection in the Scenic City. Over the years, the department grew alongside Chattanooga’s booming population and industrial footprint. Today, at 155 years strong, the Chattanooga Fire Department operates with more than 400 sworn personnel working out of twenty stations across the city. The CFD functions as an all-hazards emergency response agency, providing advanced fire suppression & rescue, specialized technical rescue, emergency medical response, and fire prevention & community risk reduction.  Across 155 years, the tools have changed—from leather buckets and steam boilers to thermal imaging cameras, aerial ladders, and specialized rescue equipment—but the core mission has remained constant. Generations of Chattanooga firefighters have answered the call with courage, professionalism, and an unwavering commitment to protecting lives and property across the Scenic City. We pay tribute to all of our firefighters- past and present- as we continue to pave the way for the future.

As Executive Director of the Family Justice Center, I have the great honor of working alongside an incredibly talented and dedicated team of staff, partners, and supporters who pour their hearts into making a difference in our community. ❤️ The past few weeks have been a whirlwind, but they’ve reminded me just how blessed I am to do this work with such amazing people! Such a wonderful celebration of local entrepreneurs, with absolutely amazing food and desserts from talented participants in KIC’s program! From Washington, D.C., to international conversations and celebrating the talent in our own backyard, these past few weeks have reinforced something I deeply believe: relationships matter, collaboration makes us stronger, and amazing things happen when people come together for their community. And while I’ve had the privilege of representing the FJC at these events, our incredible staff continues the important work every single day, walking alongside survivors, educating our community, and coordinating responses that strengthen victim safety and offender accountability. I couldn’t be prouder or more grateful for this team’s dedication, compassion, and commitment! I’m so thankful for the friendships, partnerships, and opportunities this work brings, but most of all, for the amazing people I get to share this journey with. Department: WW - Solid Waste Handling SERIES LEVEL: The Plant Operator 2 is the second level of a four-level wastewater plant operations series. ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS: (The following duties ARE NOT intended to serve as a comprehensive list of all duties performed by all employees in this classification, only a representative summary of the primary duties and responsibilities. Incumbent(s) may not be required to perform all duties listed and may be required to perform additional, position-specific duties.) Maintains, operates, and checks the operation of all collection systems, lift stations, and chlorination facilities; operates pumps, valves, and other equipment by hand or mechanical means to regulate the flow of wastewater through various primary and secondary treatment processes; maintains an even flow to assure maximum efficiency of plant equipment and compliance with regulatory requirements. Operates multiple pump stations, which include station maintenance, emergency repair, and response; data collection, record-keeping, and sample collection. Collects samples of wastewater and other materials at scheduled times; performs standardized control tests; operates, adjusts, and maintains chemical feed equipment to ensure compliance with established standards; performs record-keeping functions such as logging plant operations, test results, maintenance work, and unusual operating conditions encountered; prepares special reports as required. Reads and monitors meters, gauges, charts, instruments, and computerized systems to identify potential problems and ensure continuous operations; changes recording charts and ensures their continuous operation. Performs routine and higher-level maintenance at plant facilities and grounds, including washing down the facility daily, maintaining grounds such as cutting grass and light maintenance duties, the sludge handling facilities including odor control and performing general housekeeping duties; performs maintenance of plant machinery, equipment, piping, and structures; cleans air diffusers, clears blockages from pipes and valves, and performs repairs as necessary. Prepares and records a variety of readings and information related to plant operations in applicable logbooks. May ensure that all daily samples, Chains-of-Custody, and Daily Reports correctly follow the State and Federal regulations before preparing and disseminating a variety of routine and legally mandated reports related to wastewater plant operations. Routine duties involve highly skilled work of operating, maintaining, and monitoring wastewater (sludge) flows and stabilization in the treatment plant. Specifically in solids, it involves the operation of high-volume, high-speed centrifuges in order to recycle the sludge into usable organic fertilizer. Utilize computerized graphic displays for Centrifuges, conveyors, pumps, plus controlled chemical mixing and injection; then verify and interpret the process and direct proper personnel to resolve any problems, ensuring efficient and safe plant operations. May perform skilled technical work in the operation of the Moccasin Bend Wastewater Treatment Plant, utilizing a bank of four computer monitors, monitoring all 88 pump stations and CSO’s from a secure location. May observe, maintain, and provide Situational awareness to remote facilities operations via SCADA in order to control equipment, conditions, and personnel during a 12-hour rotating shift. Coordinate operational failures with the maintenance and Electrical departments or other agencies as required. May coordinate with other departments, vendors, and Contractors for access to secure work sites. May maintain contact via Radio/ phone communication with outside workers and contractors. May conduct site visits after normal work hours as needed in case of loss of communication, station failure, or unforeseen problems as they arise. If unable to troubleshoot/ repair problems in a timely manner, contact the on-call operator, mechanic, or electrician as needed. May operate a City vehicle to carry out duties at pump stations throughout the city. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers, and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. Performs other duties as assigned. This position is deemed essential during inclement weather situations and must report to or remain at work, even when administrative closings are announced, as determined by the Department Head. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: High School Diploma or GED supplemented by vocational/technical training in wastewater treatment plant operations' or a related field and six (6) months of work experience in a wastewater treatment plant, operating chemical processing equipment, clarifiers, collecting and lab testing samples, sludge inventory, adjusting flows and/or reading meters; or any equivalent combination of education, training/experience sufficient to successfully perform the essential duties of the job. OR High School diploma or GED with six (6) months of water or wastewater operations experience and a Grade II Moccasin Bend Environmental Campus Wastewater Certification. This is a career ladder position. This position will receive an automatic progression to Plant Operator 3 when the incumbent has achieved the required minimum qualifications and licenses/certifications for the next position in the series. LICENSING AND CERTIFICATIONS: Valid Driver’s License KNOWLEDGE AND SKILLS: Knowledge of operation, maintenance and repair of wastewater plant equipment and facilities; wastewater treatment principles, methods and practices; operation and maintenance of a wide variety of tools and equipment utilized in the trade; mathematical concepts; safety rules, codes and regulations and safe work methods and precautions related to the work; methods and precautions in storing and handling chlorine and other hazardous gasses and chemicals; routine process control tests; and preventative maintenance practices and procedures as applied to wastewater treatment facilities and collection systems. Skill in operating wastewater treatment plant equipment; performing routine maintenance and making operating adjustments to wastewater equipment; cleaning facilities and equipment; recognizing unusual, inefficient or dangerous operating conditions and taking appropriate action; reading and recording data from gauges and meters; performing routine control tests and adjust plant equipment accordingly; preparing and maintaining a variety of records and logs of work performed; and communication and interpersonal skills as applied to interaction with coworkers, supervisor, and the general public, sufficient to exchange or convey information and to receive work direction. PHYSICAL DEMANDS: Positions in this class typically require climbing, balancing, stooping, kneeling, crouching, reaching, standing, walking, pushing, pulling, lifting, fingering, grasping, feeling, talking, hearing, and seeing. WORK ENVIRONMENT: Medium Work: Exerting up to 50 pounds of force occasionally and/or up to 20 pounds of force frequently and/or up to 10 pounds of force constantly to move objects. Incumbents may be subjected to moving mechanical parts, electrical currents, vibrations, fumes, odors, dusts, gases, poor ventilation, chemicals, oils, extreme temperatures, inadequate lighting, work space restrictions, intense noises, and travel. Chattanooga Police Department Retires K9 Baba CHATTANOOGA, Tenn.  –  After years of dedicated service, the Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) announces the retirement of K9 Baba, a decorated explosives detection and patrol dog. K9 Baba, a 7-year-old German Shepherd, retired after 5 years with CPD. During her distinguished career, K9 Baba performed several hundred sweeps for explosives and located more than 30 firearms, keeping the community and visitors to the Scenic City safe.  K9 Baba worked numerous high-profile events, including the FIFA World Cup, IRONMAN 70.3 and 140.6, Moon River, and the Blue Cross Bowl. K9 Baba also enjoyed locating suspects and assisting patrol, investigative units, and federal partners. Outside of Chattanooga, K9 Baba earned recognition for her exceptional performance at competitions. Most recently, she was named "Top Dog" at the 2025 United States Police Canine Association (USPCA) Region 22 explosives trials. In 2024, K9 Baba and her handler, Officer John Isler, claimed second place in the American Tactical K9 Association Best Team Competition. The Chattanooga Police Department thanks K9 Baba for her time with the department and recognizes the commitment of her handler (Ofc Isler), his family, and community members who support the K9 Unit. The Chattanooga Police Department wishes K9 Baba a long, healthy retirement.

One of our team member, David Collins, shares his son's NYC Marathon experience. 😊 "As a proud dad, I couldn’t be more excited to share the incredible accomplishment of my 27-year-old son, Mike, who recently completed the 50th Anniversary TCS New York City Marathon! This was Mike’s third marathon, following previous finishes in the St. Jude Marathon in Memphis and the Charlotte Marathon. Running 26.2 miles through the streets of New York City is an extraordinary challenge, but being part of such a historic milestone made it even more special. What makes the accomplishment even sweeter is that Mike crossed the finish line in just over 4 hours and 30 minutes, recording his fastest marathon time yet and setting a new personal record! What many people don’t realize is that running a marathon is about much more than the 26.2 miles on race day. It takes months of preparation, discipline, and an incredible commitment to training. We’re talking countless hours of running, early mornings, long miles, and pushing through when your body is telling you otherwise. In the final weeks leading up to the race, Mike was tackling grueling 15- to 20-mile training runs a few times a month before the marathon. That’s a level of dedication and determination that is difficult to appreciate unless you’ve experienced it. As his parents, we couldn’t be prouder. Watching him set ambitious goals, put in the work, and see it all come together on one of the world’s biggest marathon stages is incredibly rewarding. At just 27 years old, Mike has already accomplished something most people would never attempt, much less complete three times. His mom and I are beyond proud of him, and we look forward to seeing what challenge he takes on next!" David Collins, Admin Manager for City Wide Services

🐾🇺🇸 PAWS OFF! PURPOSE ON! 🇺🇸🐾 A working service dog is not simply a dog wearing a vest. They are someone’s independence, safety, freedom, and sometimes even their lifeline. When you see a service dog in public, you may see an adorable face, a wagging tail, and a beautiful animal you’d love to pet. But what you may not see is the invisible disability, the countless hours of specialized training, or the life-changing tasks that dog has been trained to perform. ❤️ That service dog has a job to do, and that job matters! Service dogs assist individuals with a wide range of disabilities, including mobility limitations, neurological conditions, seizure disorders, PTSD, vision loss, and many other visible and invisible disabilities. A moment of distraction may seem harmless, but it could prevent a service dog from recognizing an important medical change, responding to an emergency, or helping their handler remain safe. 🐾 So how can YOU help? Simply respect the working partnership. Don’t pet, call, whistle at, feed, or distract a working service dog. Give the team room to navigate safely, and always speak directly to the handler rather than trying to engage the dog. And remember, not every disability is visible. Someone should never have to explain their medical history to receive kindness, dignity, and respect. As Mrs. Chattanooga America, my platform, Accessibility for All, is about more than awareness. It’s about education, advocacy, inclusion, and ensuring that individuals with disabilities have the same opportunities to participate fully in everyday life. Service dogs aren’t accessories. They aren’t entertainment. They are highly trained working partners who help make independence possible. 🇺🇸 And for our veterans who rely on service dogs, these extraordinary partnerships can mean renewed confidence, greater independence, and the freedom to reclaim parts of life they once thought were lost. Accessibility begins with awareness, but real inclusion begins with ACTION. 🐾 Here’s my challenge to you: The next time you see a working service dog, admire that beautiful partnership from a respectful distance. Your kindness may be the very thing that allows that team to do its job safely. ❤️ PLEASE SHARE THIS POST! You never know who may need this reminder. One share can educate someone, change a perspective, and help protect a working service dog team. Because accessibility isn’t a privilege. It’s a right. 👑 Mrs. Chattanooga America 2026 🐾 Accessibility for All Paws Off! Purpose On! Warrior Freedom Service DogsThe Dog Wizard Chattanooga John Hayes Mayor’s Council on Disability

Wednesday, we held our annual Staff Appreciation Lunch to honor the incredible team behind Chattanooga Parks and Outdoors! 🌳✨ None of our successes would be possible without the dedicated people who show up every single day to serve our community. From Recreation and Parks Maintenance to Natural Resources, Outdoor Chattanooga, Therapeutic Recreation, Sports Outreach, and beyond—every team member plays a vital role in making Chattanooga a better place to live, work, and play. Every day, our staff brings smiles to families across the city, in our parks, on our fields, and through our programs. Whether it’s a child’s first home run, a new skill learned on the water, a playground discovery, or the protection of a native species, their impact reaches every corner of our city. Thank you all for your hard work, dedication, and passion. You make a difference every single day, and Chattanooga is better because of it. We're proud of this team and grateful for everything you do! Please join us in giving a special shoutout to our 2026 Award Winners: 🏆 Employee of the Year: James "Bo" Walker (Recreation) Unanimously chosen by the team as the "GLUE" of Recreation and truly "CLUTCH." Bo is a tournament favorite who consistently steps up for weekend shifts, solves problems, and serves our community with a smile. 🏛️ Administrator's Award: Zach Hull (Riverparks Superintendent) Honored for visionary leadership and steadfast commitment—guiding his team through the Walnut Street Bridge construction, droughts, and major events while keeping Chattanooga’s iconic parks exceeding expectations. ⚡ Urgency Award: Cameron Gallina (Parks Maintenance) Always quick to tackle a new job without any question, Cameron works tirelessly to plant and care for the beautiful native flowers blooming across town and at City Hall. 🧩 Problem Solver Award: Juana Tomas (Recreation) The behind-the-scenes hero of Watkins Street, Juana seamlessly coordinates facility needs, work orders, IT support, and customer service across multiple divisions. 🤝 Team Player Award: Austin Adderholt (Communications) A bridge-builder across all divisions who leads volunteer recruitment, drives employee engagement, and stepped up big to support communications this year. 💡 Innovation Award: Marcus Thomas (Recreation) Modernized our sports divisions by streamlining registrations, introducing live game tracking, and designing a new youth basketball format that saves city dollars while giving families a better experience. 💙 Customer Service Award: Bill Durkin (Outdoor Chattanooga) Simply outstanding when it comes to welcoming visitors. Bill treats every participant on our outdoor outings with warmth, care, and a huge smile. 🌟 Part-Time Full Impact Award: Josephine "Josie" Hemmer (Outdoor Chattanooga) Brings infectious positive energy and reliability to every program she is a part of—leaving a full-time mark on our city far beyond her scheduled hours. 🌱 Chattanooga Tree Project Spotlight: Holly Odell (Natural Resources) The ultimate unsung hero who handles the essential, behind-the-scenes administrative work that keeps the Chattanooga Tree Project running smoothly. Thank you to our entire staff for your passion, hard work, and dedication. Chattanooga is better every single day because of you! 💚 #Chattanooga #ChattanoogaParks #StaffAppreciation #CommunityFirst #Nooga #TeamChattanooga

CPD Investigating Shooting on Airpark Drive CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is investigating a shooting that occurred on Airpark Drive Monday night. At approximately 7:00 p.m., CPD responded to a reported shooting at a hotel in the 6200 block of Airpark Drive. Upon arrival, officers discovered that both the victim and the suspect had left the scene. The victim, a 22-year-old male, was found at a hospital with non-life threatening injuries. CPD's Homicide and Crime Scene Units responded to investigate and process the scene. Investigators are actively following all leads.  The information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. The Chattanooga Police Department asks anyone with information regarding this incident to call 423-698-2525. #CPDnews
